newsitem.title: CANADA: Tories claim to be sole option for united Canada.
newsitem.headline: Tories claim to be sole option for united Canada.

text.p: Canadian Tory leader Jean Charest is playing his trump cards this weekend as the Canadian election campaign heads into its final round.
Charest is criss-crossing Quebec, Canada's populous French-speaking province, aiming to build momentum to the June 2 election by painting himself as the only person who can keep Canada united.
"It's leadership I offer you ... It's determination to make this country work," he said on Friday in a campaign speech to about 100 boisterous Quebeckers in Saint-Hyacinthe, east of Montreal.

"We are the only political party capable of rallying support in every region in Canada," Charest added later to a smaller crowd in Victoriaville, near Quebec City, where separatist support has been strong.

Charest is banking on his personal popularity to propel his party from its measly two seats in the current Parliament. The energetic 38-year-old has consistently come out on top in polls that measure confidence in leadership abilities.

A Leger and Leger poll published on Saturday in the Journal de Montreal showed 43 percent of decided Quebeckers say he is their favourite leader, compared to 17 percent for Liberal Jean Chretien and 18 percent for separatist Bloc Quebecois leader Gilles Duceppe.

But realistically, Charest cannot hope for more than second place. With the reigning Liberals comfortably ahead in the polls countrywide, official opposition is the big prize in the June 2 Canadian election.

Charest's Conservatives stand a decent chance. Charest's star has soared since his strong performance in televised debates last week. The Tories are neck and neck with the Liberals and the Bloc Quebecois in Quebec, Canada's second-biggest province.
But the Leger and Leger poll on Saturday showed that support for Charest in Quebec is soft, and about one third of Quebec voters are undecided.

Charest has to build momentum on a two-day swing through his home province, playing up his charm and appealing to voters as the only leader with enough national support to fix Canada's precarious national unity.
"He's the best of the lot," said one housewife who came out to see Charest at a stop in Drummondville, between Montreal and Quebec City. "He's our man," she said with a wink.

While there are five parties running for re-election on June 2, only three of them have a presence in Quebec: the ruling Liberals, the Tories and the Bloc Quebecois, a separatist Quebec-based party that forms the official opposition.

But the separatist campaign has gone from bad to worse. Leader Duceppe stumbled repeatedly, contradicting himself and other prominent separatists with unclear messages. As the campaign started up, he showed up on national television wearing an unflattering shower cap while touring a cheese factory. The first week of the campaign ended with Duceppe firing the driver of his media bus for getting lost.
"Imagine if he were driving a country," one grandmother in Drummondville said.

Duceppe has called in separatist reinforcements, most notably the charismatic provincial Premier Lucien Bouchard, who in 1995 boosted lagging support for separatism so that the separatists came within 1 percent of winning a pro- sovereignty referendum.
But Bouchard was leader of the federal Bloc Quebecois at the time. Now, as premier, he has made major cutbacks to shake up Quebec's finances, putting his following at risk.

"The separatists have made unbearable cuts. Bouchard cut our health care and (Prime Minister) Chretien cut my pension," complained 72-year-old Charest-supporter Gilberte Racine in Saint-Hyacinthe. "They don't want us to live well. It makes no sense."
Charest is tapping into the discontent in Quebec, telling voters who are tired of fighting Ottawa that he will bring stability and prosperity to politics.

"Now is an opportunity to rid ourselves of this hidden tax on the Canadian and Quebec economy, this hidden tax of political uncertainty that has slowed us down, that has broken our appetites and our dreams, that has affected everyone in the province of Quebec," Charest thundered in a campaign speech. "This hidden tax ... costs us higher interest rates, this hidden tax costs us jobs and investment."
Canada's unemployment rate has hovered stubbornly between 9 and 10 percent for the past two years, with Quebec's rate above the national average.

While Charest's appeal to Quebeckers' uncertainty over jobs is bound to hit home, the Tory leader risks splitting the pro-unity vote with Chretien, letting the Bloc Quebecois slide up the middle for votes.
